problemStatement.formal:
Is it true that for all large $n$ there exists $k$ such that $n+k$ is composite and\[p(n+k)>k^2,\]where $p(m)$ is the least prime factor of $m$?



Related to questions of Erd\H{o}s, Eggleton, and Selfridge. This may be true with $k^2$ replaced by $k^d$ for any $d$.

See also [680] and [682].

d1_at_2_mod_3: d=1 via k=3 for primes p ≡ 2 mod 3 (proved)
insights: k=1 trivially resolves the conjecture for ALL d whenever n+1 is composite (p(m) >= 2 > 1^d)
The conjecture is open ONLY for n where n+1 is prime (n = p-1 for some prime p)
For k >= 2: the constraint forces k^(2d) < n+k, bounding k to roughly n^(1/(2d))
The d=0 case is trivially true (k=n gives 2n composite, p(2n) >= 2 > 1)
Connected to problems 680 (p(n+k) > k^2+1) and 682 (rough numbers in prime gaps, solved by Gafni-Tao 2025)
Infrastructure is complete: leastPrimeFactor, IsLeastPrimeFactor, uniqueness, sqrt bound all proved from Mathlib
When n+1 is an odd prime (n >= 2), any witness k >= 2 must be odd: even offsets give minFac = 2 <= k^d
For primes p ≡ 2 (mod 3) with p+2 composite, k=3 witnesses d=1 since minFac(n+3) >= 5 > 3
nextSteps: The open part: prove existence of k for n with n+1 prime (requires sieve theory or prime gap bounds)
Connect to Cramér conjecture: if gaps are O(log²p), then k can be bounded
Investigate computational evidence for small n with n+1 prime
